catalog_quote: The placement of the stress in an isolated word in Jewish Gabes does not differ from other Maghrebi dialects. Nonetheless, as has been observed by Cohen (1975, 84), there is a conspicuous discrepancy between the Jewish and Muslim dialects of Tunis, where Muslim speakers pronounce much stronger stress than Jewish speakers, the stress in the latter case being hardly audible. It is worth noting that the stress in Jewish Gabes, as in other North African dialects of Arabic, is mobile, namely, it can change its position in a word when the syllable structure is changed due to an agglutination of affixes or the negation particle, e.g., māt́ət 'she died' > mā mātə́tš 'she did not die'. The rules established by Cohen (1975, 85) regarding the stress in an isolated word in Jewish Tunis are also relevant to Jewish Gabes. According to these rules, the ultimate syllable is stressed either when it cont…
sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title (El Zarka 2012, STUF) is a misfiled Glottolog reference: its Crossref abstract shows it treats Moroccan and Egyptian modal particles, not Tunisian word stress; paywalled, priority none. The real yield of this search of works with stress in the title is Talmoudi 1980, The Arabic Dialect of Susa (Tunisia), previously still-to-obtain as print-only and now found open on archive.org (mis-titled upload), downloaded with text layer to Its sec. 1.2.2 (pp. 42-43, page images verified) states a first-syllable / leftmost-long-vowel primary-stress rule with antepenult outputs (gèn:ériy:a, lì:litkum, sqò:fe:tu), which keeps the catalog's weight-sensitive kind but contradicts the deciding Gebski/Cohen 'final superheavy, else penult' rule for a Muslim sedentary sister lect of tuni1259. Not proposed as superseding source (different lect, rule diverges from the Tunis cross-check); Singer 1984 (Tunis Medina, De Gruyter paywalled) becomes the high-priority acquisition to settle the language-level rule, Cohen 1975 medium. Peace Corps courses on ERIC (ED183018 text layer, ED401742 and ED402739 image-only, fronts read) are silent/not scanned, low priority; Inglefield 1970 (ED043013) has no ERIC full text. Gebski 2024 catalog quote re-verified verbatim in the copy we hold. all lookups used direct downloads and APIs.

new_statements.quote: 1.2.2.1 If a word is made up of a string of syllables with a short vowel, i.e. V, CV, CVC, CCV, CCVC, CVCC, CCVCC, CCCVC or CCCVCC, the first syllable receives the primary (`) and the second the secondary stress (´). [hàmrá] red (fem.) [...] [gèn:ériy:a] artichoke [...] 1.2.2.2 If a word comprises only one syllable with long vowel this receives primary stress if it is not the last syllable in the word. [ʕà:lim] scholar [...] [lì:litkum] your night. 1.2.2.3 If a word contains two syllables or more with a long vowel, the first gets primary stress. [sqò:fe:tu] his ceilings

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive (long vowels attract) but left-oriented: primary stress on the first syllable of all-short-vowel words (antepenult in trisyllables), otherwise on the leftmost non-final long-vowel syllable; epenthetic schwa never stressed. First-hand, from a Muslim sedentary Sahil lect (Medina of Susa) under tuni1259. It agrees with the catalog's 'weight' kind but contradicts the deciding quote's 'final if superheavy, else penult' rule (right window, default penult) for this sister lect; the record's Tunis-koine cross-check (Wikipedia/Gibson) still sides with Gebski/Cohen.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Reader's bearing stands; three refinements. (1) Talmoudi's weight is vowel length ONLY: rule 1.2.2.1 lists CVC, CVCC, CCVCC, CCCVCC among the 'short vowel' syllables that take the initial-primary pattern, so a Susa what counts as heavy would be 'CVV only', not the catalog's superheavy CVVC/CVCC. (2) Rule 1.2.2.2 gives the lone long-vowel syllable primary stress 'if it is not the last syllable in the word' and is silent on where primary goes when the only long vowel IS final (no CVC.CV:C example anywhere in secs. 1.2.2.1-1.2.2.4); by the 1.2.2.1 default it would be initial, the mirror image of…

sources.note: First-hand description of the Muslim sedentary Medina-of-Susa lect (Sahil; under tuni1259). Stress is quantity-conditioned but LEFT-oriented: in all-short-vowel words primary stress is on the first syllable (secondary on the second), so trisyllables come out antepenult ([gèn:ériy:a] 'artichoke', [èrénbik] 'your rabbit'); the first long-vowel syllable takes primary stress provided it is not word-final ([ʕà:lim], [ktibnè:lu], [lì:litkum], [sqò:fe:tu]); epenthetic schwa is never stressed ([ləqfìl] 'the lock', final CVC stressed). sources.quote: 'Lexical stress placement in Arabic varies from standard to dialect and from one dialect to another but is in all cases fixed stress conditioned by syllabic weight.' Test material: 'Two sets of 10 disyllabic Tunisian Arabic near minimal pairs of the kind: /ˈbeddel/ ~ /bedˈdelt/ were used ... /ˈbeddel/ he changed ... /bedˈdelt/ I changed' (penult stress with final CVC, final stress with final CVCC). Acoustic result: duration is not a correlate of lexical stress in TA, only of accent.

sources.quote: 'Ein jedes an irgend ein Wort antretendes Suffix verlangt, dass die vorhergehende Silbe den Ton erhaelt. Treten zwei Suffixe an, so wird im Komplexe also das erste Suffix betont.' and 'Die Betonung, die ein Wort oder eine Wortform im Tunisischen hat, ist im Allgemeinen fest. Dennoch ist der Accent nicht so unerschuetterlich, dass nicht bisweilen das Bestreben nach Rhythmus Accentuationen ... veraenderte.' No compact syllable-weight rule is stated; stress is given per paradigm. Consistent with mobile stress recomputed after suffixation; silent on the superheavy-final clause as such.
